newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain Basques meet to show unity against ETA.
newsitem.headline: Spain Basques meet to show unity against ETA.

text.p: Political parties of Spain's Basque region met to discuss a common approach to separatist violence on Friday, deeply divided on the key issues of talks with the rebel group ETA and where ETA prisoners should serve jail terms.
The parties were meeting as the Ajuria Enea pact, a forum set up in 1988 to seek the "pacification and normalisation" of the troubled Basque region in the north.
They hope to find some sort of consensus on how to respond to a resurgence of violence in which four people have been killed in the past two weeks, presumably by ETA guerrillas.
"What we have to try to do is reclaim once again the unity of Ajuria Enea," Carlos Iturgaiz, the ruling Popular Party's leader in the Basque region, said before entering the meeting.

Basque President Jose Antonio Ardanza is expected to reintroduce a conditional offer of dialogue with ETA which his Basque National Party (PNV) first made last June, two days after the rebels declared a unilateral, one-week truce.
The proposal could be rejected by the Basque branch of Spanish Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar's Popular Party.

The PP is one of six parties in the Ajuria Enea pact along with Basque Nationalists and the regional branch of the opposition Socialist party. Herri Batasuna, the politican arm of ETA, is the only parliamentary party not in the pact.

Ardanza's offer of dialogue is linked to a cessation of violence, a position in line with the PP. But government ministers in Madrid have made clear they do not think the timing is right for any talk of negotiations.
Politicians and analysts say the division between the Basque Nationalist parties on the one hand and the PP and Socialists on the other creates fertile ground for violence.
"ETA would last 10 minutes if the parties advance in Ajuria Enea," Interior Minister Jaime Mayor Oreja said recently.
Even within the Basque Nationalist camp, there are deep rifts on whether to press for negotiations with ETA now that it has stepped up attacks.
Basque Interior Minister Juan Maria Atutxa said ahead of the meeting he was hopeful Ardanza's proposal would win the support of Ajuria Enea even though it was rejected last June.

"Certain offers in certain moments do not have an effect but, at best, they could have an effect now and be accepted because in these months we have been living in situations which make people reflect in a different way," Atutxa told Reuters in an interview on Thursday.
Speaking at the seat of the Basque regional government in Vitoria, Atutxa said the Ajuria Enea pact had been rendered ineffective in recent few years.
While Basque nationalists have pursued a more conciliatory stance toward Herri Batasuna, the Popular Party was taking a firm line on ETA to draw voters in its 1996 election campaign.
The Basque nationalists and the PP also clash over where more than 500 ETA prisoners should serve out their terms.
Madrid has stuck by a policy of "dispersion", started under the former Socialist government, under which prisoners are spread all over Spain in small groups.
The Basque parliament approved an initiative on Thursday calling for the transfer of all Basque prisoners, including ETA members, to jails within 300 km (200 miles) of the Basque country.

The regional PP and Socialist parties rejected the initiative which also proposed sending a parliamentary delegation to present the idea to a minister in Madrid and to the jailed leader of ETA prisoners Juan Lorenza Lasa Mitxelena.
"What (the proposal) is trying to do is disunite the Ajuria Enea," the PP's Iturgaiz said.
